gaps: Boundary semantics for a symlink that lives INSIDE the target but resolves OUTSIDE it were unspecified. The plan's 'a legal run is unchanged' claim (AC5) hinges on whether such a write is refused or allowed, and the two readings diverge on real behaviour.

AC4 asks for 'a regression test the recurring repository-escape class cannot silently reopen', but named no mechanism. A per-site behavioural test only covers the sites that exist today — a future unguarded write would pass it, which is exactly how this class recurred five times.
resolutions: Human ruling (Symlink rule = 'Refuse — outside is outside'): a destination whose resolved path lands outside the target is refused however it is reached, including through an in-target symlink pointing out; resolve(strict=False) is not special-cased. A legal init/adopt/upgrade never writes through such a link, so refusing cannot break a real run. Folded into Technical Approach (Boundary semantics) and the helper's unit tests (in-target-symlink-pointing-outside case).

Human ruling (Anti-reopen = 'Structural scan + per-site tests'): AC4 is met by the per-site behavioural escape tests PLUS a structural scan that reads init/adopt/upgrade and fails if any raw filesystem-mutating call appears outside the shared helper, so a FUTURE unguarded site fails the suite. Folded into AC4 proof and Task 1 scope.
summary: The plan is unusually thorough; most decisions are already settled and justified with rejected-alternatives. Two genuinely-open, high-consequence decisions surfaced — the in-target-symlink boundary semantics (correctness crux for 'legal run unchanged') and the anti-reopen test mechanism (durability crux, whether the consolidation sticks). Both were put to the human and ruled toward the stronger option, then folded into the plan body. No contradictions with active decisions or the accepted 0028. Ready for plan-mode approval.
